title: Ep 287: From Ravel Cofounder to Knowable CEO, Nik Reed Has Learned that Building Quality AI for Legal Takes A Lot of Hard Work
author: Nik Reed

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Reed shifts the emphasis away from end-to-end delivery redesign and pricing or apprenticeship disruption. He frames AI mainly as making established analytical work more accessible and restoring lawyers’ capacity for critical reasoning, while treating radical billable-hour implications as speculative.
qs: And if you go back to like Lex Machina in the early days, you know, Moneyball for Lawyers, I think what we were wrong with, we're not changing what lawyers do, maybe, because lawyers aren't going to become baseball players anytime soon.

But maybe what AI allows us to do is it allows lawyers to do what they always were supposed to be doing, that which they want to do, and that we're happy to pay them for, which is critical reasoning, using the intelligence that you develop in law school and years of practice to solve really hard problems because technology created an imbalance.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Reed supports supervised AI and continued lawyer judgment, and he assumes expertise develops through years of practice. However, he does not address whether automating junior work will disrupt that development pathway or propose reconstructed apprenticeship, so his position on the cluster’s principal training-risk proposition cannot be determined.
qs: But maybe what AI allows us to do is it allows lawyers to do what they always were supposed to be doing, that which they want to do, and that we're happy to pay them for, which is critical reasoning, using the intelligence that you develop in law school and years of practice to solve really hard problems because technology created an imbalance.
And then fundamentally, we're still the decision makers.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: Reed discusses AI-enabled lawyer productivity, accessible analytics and potentially higher hourly value, but does not address whether adoption can expand meaningful legal help or close the justice gap. His claims therefore do not establish a position on the cluster’s access-to-justice proposition.
qs: And it's because lawyers will be able to do so much more with their time.
Whether or not that comes to fruition, we'll see.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: Reed supports the premise that AI can make labour-intensive legal analysis more accessible and may increase lawyers’ output and value. However, he does not address the cluster’s central explanation that adoption depends on organisational redesign, leadership, incentives, frontline resources, connected data and professional identity; cultural adoption appears only as an unanswered question.
qs: And so the idea was, could we put that at your fingertips?
Whether or not that comes to fruition, we'll see.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: Reed accepts the shift from answer generation to task completion and materially develops the cluster’s orchestration and autonomy themes: he advocates coordinating specialised models rather than relying on a universal assistant, while limiting delegation to discrete, lower-stakes tasks. He also reinforces the need for sustained engineering and supervision, though he does not directly substantiate error propagation or quantify verification costs.
qs: And using multiple models, figuring out what some models are better at than other, using them together in the right way to get it to work.
I think it's exciting, again, for very discrete, defined tasks that aren't bet the farm kind of things.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: Reed accepts the cluster’s core proposition and materially develops it with practitioner-specific requirements: curated document sets and metadata, collaboration between lawyers and data scientists, specialist task-focused systems, and continuing supervision and maintenance. He also reinforces retained human judgment while treating productivity gains as prospective rather than established.
qs: I think if you have a very pristine and closed environment, so that means not a lot of duplicates, you've got the final document that matters, you've got really good metadata that you can infuse into the LLM as questions are being asked, and you still need a team of lawyers and data scientists working together to inform.
So I think we have to remember that with AI, you still need to do a lot of work around the generative AI.

st.t: Contract intelligence: Business coordination exceeds document storage
st.an: Reed accepts that useful contract AI must do more than sit atop a document repository and materially develops the cluster’s proposition through operational knowledge, specialised tooling and continuous answer-quality control. His examples show how AI can make controlling terms across complex contract families usable, though he focuses more on contract analysis than cross-department business coordination.
qs: I do, you know, without naming competitors or potential competitors, I think it is a fallacy to believe that just because you drop Generative AI on top of a repository, all of a sudden, you're going to do all of these things that we've all been trying to do for a really long time really well.
And if you infuse the LLMs with the knowledge of those operations behind the scenes, when someone's asking a question, the answers are like startlingly good.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Reed accepts the importance of legal-specific context and materially develops the cluster’s lawyer–engineer collaboration claim through Knowable’s contract-focused product experience. He explains specialist value as combining enterprise-contract knowledge with software and AI expertise, while stressing deliberate multidisciplinary development. His account does not establish verification practices or comparative performance.
qs: And so they spun it out with LexisNexis, where Lexis had the software and AI knowledge, and the Knowable team had all this knowledge about contracts in large enterprise and what people at large enterprises needed to know about their contracts.
It's the work where lawyers and data scientists and product managers and engineers are teaching each other, learning from each other.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: Reed accepts the cluster’s core emphasis on use-case discipline, legal context and deliberate implementation, and materially extends it with a concrete orchestration model in which an interface routes questions among specialised AI services rather than relying on one universal model. His productivity claims remain explicitly conditional, consistent with the synthesis’s caution about transformation claims, though he offers little direct evidence on human verification.
qs: And so I think, yeah, for all of our listeners, hopefully you're being thoughtful about these things and using products for what they're intended to do and still really trying to nail use cases that you have.
And it does a lot of things, but maybe the most important thing is just deciding which service it needs to get to to answer the question that you've asked.

st.t: Adoption leadership: Trust must follow customer outcomes
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s conditional optimism: Reed recommends experimenting with AI while remaining careful, and both speakers offer broad expectations of adoption and progress rather than demonstrated customer outcomes or empirical evidence.
qs: It doesn't mean we don't have to be careful, consider it.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: Reed supports selective, use-case-led adoption rather than indiscriminate pursuit of new AI capabilities. His emphasis on matching products and underlying services to concrete needs aligns with the cluster’s practical filtering and strategy themes, though he does not substantially address continuous learning or shared knowledge infrastructure.
qs: And so I think, yeah, for all of our listeners, hopefully you're being thoughtful about these things and using products for what they're intended to do and still really trying to nail use cases that you have.
And it does a lot of things, but maybe the most important thing is just deciding which service it needs to get to to answer the question that you've asked.

st.t: Legal platforms: Content and governance differentiate workflows
st.an: Reed supports the cluster’s core proposition that legal-AI differentiation lies in use-case-specific orchestration rather than a single universal model. He describes Protégé as routing questions among multiple AI services and tentatively attributes an advantage to large providers, while offering architectural reasoning rather than measured performance evidence. He does not address the cluster’s human-verification proposition.
qs: And it does a lot of things, but maybe the most important thing is just deciding which service it needs to get to to answer the question that you've asked.

And so that's kind of why I said, you know, that those biggest companies are probably in the best position to do this well, because not because they're just going to create one LLM to solve everything.

st.t: Pragmatic adoption: Experimentation outruns transformation evidence
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: it advocates careful experimentation while expressing optimism about broad future adoption. Its claims remain predictions and recommendations rather than evidence of demonstrated organisational transformation or measured outcomes.
qs: A few of them are already out there, and hopefully people are more excited and scared this time around because I think we're all going to be using it if we're not already.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: Reed supports the cluster’s copilot framing: AI can accelerate context-heavy legal analysis, while lawyers retain responsibility for judgment and advice. His contextual, relational-data account also aligns with the view that value requires more than raw model access, although he does not substantially address organisation-wide workflow redesign, readiness, verification or measured adoption outcomes. He treats the dramatic billable-hour scenario as uncertain rather than established.
qs: And that's the art of being a good lawyer is understanding all this different context and then having an opinion on what actions to take or not take.
And then fundamentally, we're still the decision makers.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: Reed aligns with the cluster’s engagement-first position by encouraging practical experimentation while retaining caution. His broad optimism about adoption reinforces the agenda but adds no concrete implementation method or empirical evidence.
qs: It doesn't mean we don't have to be careful, consider it.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source supports selective augmentation by presenting generative AI as streamlining routine work and improving access to essential information so lawyers can focus on bespoke, higher-value judgment and data-informed strategy. Its support is conceptual and anecdotal rather than empirical, and it does not address verification burdens, junior development or staffing leverage.
qs: I mean, I think it's certainly what we're seeing so far in terms of applications of generative AI are applications that are streamlining a lot of that rote stuff that lawyers would have done, making it easier for them to get to essential information that they need in order to do the bespoke lawyering, to do the higher-end lawyering.
I mean, I think there has been certainly some evolution in the idea of lawyers starting to use data more strategically and thinking about cases and their approaches to cases.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Reed supports the principal proposition that AI is more likely to reduce labor-intensive production and information burdens than displace lawyers’ core value. He expects lawyers to remain valuable for critical reasoning and difficult problem-solving, although his account is predictive and does not substantively address the cluster’s broader claims about hybrid pricing, buyer-side reallocation or verification.
qs: But maybe what AI allows us to do is it allows lawyers to do what they always were supposed to be doing, that which they want to do, and that we're happy to pay them for, which is critical reasoning, using the intelligence that you develop in law school and years of practice to solve really hard problems because technology created an imbalance.
It's like, it was the thing attorneys were doing, but it was really hard, and it took armies of people in rooms, and how often could you do that?

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Reed supports selective, human-led deployment: generative AI can accelerate synthesis across complex legal information, but specialised legal products remain difficult to build and lawyers retain contextual judgment, decision-making and advisory responsibility. His preference for best-of-breed tools and cautious experimentation reinforces the cluster’s rejection of broad, automatic competence claims.
qs: I do, you know, without naming competitors or potential competitors, I think it is a fallacy to believe that just because you drop Generative AI on top of a repository, all of a sudden, you're going to do all of these things that we've all been trying to do for a really long time really well.
And that's the art of being a good lawyer is understanding all this different context and then having an opinion on what actions to take or not take.

kp.k: Reliable legal AI requires substantial interdisciplinary engineering
kp.d: Reed argues that high-quality legal AI depends on traditional machine learning, NLP, software workflows, targeted human quality control, and collaboration among lawyers, data scientists, engineers and product managers. He presents Knowable's deliberately paced generative-AI launch as an example of this work, not evidence that simply adding an LLM produces dependable legal answers.
qs: Because at the end of the day, you still need humans if you want really high quality data, especially in the law.
It's the work where lawyers and data scientists and product managers and engineers are teaching each other, learning from each other.

kp.k: Ask Knowable targets enterprise post-execution contract knowledge
kp.d: Reed distinguishes Knowable from a comprehensive contract lifecycle management platform: it organizes signed enterprise agreements and extracts metadata using machine learning with human-in-the-loop quality control. He reports that Ask Knowable is live and lets customers question their contracts in natural language. The LexisNexis North America legal team was its first alpha user; these are vendor-reported deployment descriptions, without quantified accuracy or productivity results.
qs: We are a kind of post-execution contract management and knowledge company.
So we have a whole AI engine with human-in-the-loop quality control that creates the data that we kind of extract and create from the contracts that are our clients' contracts.
Her team was the first team that we turned on to Ask Knowable.

kp.k: Clean data and metadata underpin reliable contract answers
kp.d: Reed recommends closed, deduplicated, clean document environments, high-quality metadata and use-case-specific prompt engineering. For renewal questions, he says Knowable supplies extracted expiration dates rather than asking an LLM to read 100,000 contracts; the LLM interprets the natural-language request and the system reformulates the query. His claims of greater reliability are qualitative, not benchmark findings.
qs: So that's like step one is a closed, clean environment. Make sure the data is good.
We're not just telling the LLM to go read 100,000 contracts and like come up with its answer.
We're saying, here are the expiration dates of all of these contracts.

kp.k: Contract analysis requires understanding relationships and operative hierarchy
kp.d: Reed argues that AI must be supplied with the operative relationships among master agreements, amendments, statements of work and change orders to identify controlling provisions. He describes a tool tracing successive amendments to produce a current limitation-of-liability summary, and reports that Knowable's largest client has an 800-document contract family. These are product examples, not independently tested results.
qs: amendment number three can modify amendment number two and amendment number one, but amendment one doesn't modify amendment three.
Our biggest client has an 800 document contract family, one contract, over 800 documents has just been growing over time.
And it will say, well, you know, the MSA said this, it was modified in amendment number three, amendment number four and five were silent on the issue. Amendment seven replaced the sentence in whole.

kp.k: AI shifts time from information organization toward judgment
kp.d: Reed's central augmentation argument is that AI can reduce document finding, ordering and provision identification so lawyers can focus on reasoning, advice and decisions. He frames this as restoring work lawyers were trained to perform rather than transferring final decision-making to AI. Ambrogi agrees that current applications streamline routine work and improve access to essential information; neither supplies measured time savings.
qs: if we can cut down on the amount of time lawyers spend finding and organizing to allow them to focus and reason, we have really created huge value
And then fundamentally, we're still the decision makers. We're still the advisors. We're legal counsel.

kp.k: Three waves distinguish digitization, alternative delivery, and AI
kp.d: Reed presents a framework developed with Mark Harris: the first wave changed how lawyers worked by digitizing and making information searchable; the second changed who performed work through technology-enabled alternative delivery, including Axiom and Pangea3; the third potentially changes what lawyers do through AI. He revises his earlier expectation of substantially more proactive lawyering toward restoring critical reasoning after digitization created information overload, and says the wave he identified in 2015 remains underway.
qs: The first wave was really changing how lawyers do things that they've always done before.
The second wave kind of creatively thought about changing who was doing the work.
But maybe what AI allows us to do is it allows lawyers to do what they always were supposed to be doing, that which they want to do, and that we're happy to pay them for, which is critical reasoning

kp.k: Specialization challenges the all-in-one legal AI pitch
kp.d: Ambrogi reports that Legal Week vendors increasingly positioned themselves as comprehensive workflow home bases rather than point solutions. Reed doubts that most vendors can deliver this breadth well and recommends focused products and defined use cases. He sees LexisNexis and Thomson Reuters as possible exceptions because of their data, tools and staffing. In contracting, he favors assembling best-in-class solutions across lifecycle stages while acknowledging expense and integration difficulty.
qs: you want to find a company that's really focused in trying to get one or two things right, not everything right.

Now, to Lexis and TR's credit, they're probably two of the few companies that might be able to do everything for everyone because they actually have all the data and all the tools, all the armies of engineers and lawyers.

I think it is a fallacy to believe that just because you drop Generative AI on top of a repository, all of a sudden, you're going to do all of these things that we've all been trying to do for a really long time really well.

kp.k: Legal AI requires ongoing maintenance and output evaluation
kp.d: Reed cautions law firms and corporate teams contemplating their own AI products that development is not a one-time exercise: supervision, monitoring, improvement and substantial staffing remain necessary. He cites, secondhand, Anthropic's CEO describing model-specific behavioral differences and argues that providers must continually assess answer quality as models change. This concerns software maintenance and evaluation, not a measured model-error rate.
qs: AI is still software. It has to be built. It has to be supervised. It has to be monitored. It has to be improved.

And so you want companies that are, that have armies that are paying attention to these things, that are quality ranking answers, that are paying attention to the differences in answers as the technology is evolving.

kp.k: Convincing answers can conceal errors and incomplete coverage
kp.d: Reed warns that poor input data produces bad answers that are harder to recognize because LLMs present them convincingly and may provide pleasing but incomplete responses. Ambrogi's personal example illustrates the verification gap: ChatGPT deep research produced a Massachusetts-law spreadsheet in 10 minutes, but he had not yet checked its exhaustiveness. Reed cautions against relying on an unrestricted information environment containing both accurate and inaccurate material.
qs: The scary part is that they give you bad answers very convincingly.
I haven't gone back and verified yet whether it exhaustively covered everything.
it's pulling from a lot of stuff, both accurate and inaccurate.

kp.k: Agentic systems may orchestrate specialized legal services
kp.d: Reed describes LexisNexis's assistant as an interface that directs questions to appropriate underlying AI services, rather than one LLM doing everything. Separately, he characterizes agentic AI as performing tasks rather than only retrieving information, illustrating prospective contract-renewal monitoring, document retrieval and correspondence. These examples describe an architectural argument and possible workflows, not demonstrated autonomous legal practice.
qs: it's AI that's actually completing a task. It's not just answering a question or retrieving a document for you.
maybe the most important thing is just deciding which service it needs to get to to answer the question that you've asked.
Or would you like me to send the renewal letter to company X because they're up for renewal at the end of the week or terminate this.

kp.k: Autonomous action raises control concerns for lawyers
kp.d: Reed explicitly compares AI agency with legal agency, arguing that AI agents involve ceding control to a system the lawyer did not personally teach or train. He favors narrowly defined, lower-stakes tasks and rejects courtroom substitution in the near term. This is a caution about autonomy, not an analysis of particular professional rules or liability doctrines.
qs: With AI agents, you're ceding control.
I think it's exciting, again, for very discrete, defined tasks that aren't bet the farm kind of things.
But I would not want my AI agent going to court for me anytime soon.

kp.k: Near-term associate replacement claims overstate AI capabilities
kp.d: Reed rejects the hype-driven expectation that firms can replace all associates with an AI bot within the next two years. He recommends patience, learning how to use the technology, explicit objectives and adherence to intended use cases. His alternative is conditional optimism about useful applications, not a quantified forecast of legal employment or staffing leverage.
qs: You can replace all your associates with an AI bot in the next two years, and that's not going to be true.
we still have to have really defined goals and use cases that we want the software to help us accomplish and not try to use it for things that it's not meant to do.

kp.k: Higher hourly pricing is reported as speculative
kp.d: Reed relays LexisNexis CEO Sean Fitzpatrick's suggestion that the billable hour could reach $10,000 in five years because lawyers supported by effective AI agents could deliver much more value per hour. Reed explicitly leaves the outcome uncertain. This is a reported pricing prediction, not an observed rate or Reed's firm forecast.
qs: he thinks it's quite possible that the billable hour will be $10,000 in five years.
It's because they're doing so much more and it's so valuable. Whether or not that comes to fruition, we'll see.

kp.k: Open demonstrations matter amid opaque vendor claims
kp.d: Reed calls for renewed emphasis on proving products through live demonstrations and user questions. Ambrogi reports that vendors have become less willing to provide trial credentials or unrestricted demonstrations, sometimes relying on screenshots or carefully staged queries. Their observations concern transparency and product evaluation; they do not establish comparative product performance.
qs: You couldn't fake it. You had to really be proving it and doing it.
Now they don't want to give you those passwords anymore.
sometimes they won't give you a live demo. They'll give you a very canned demo, slides and screenshots and that kind of thing

kp.k: Digitized case law may support foundation-model legal knowledge
kp.d: Ambrogi describes Ravel and Harvard's Case Law Access Project as a large-scale digitization of US case law. Reed says there is reason to believe foundation models drew legal knowledge from that resource, linking earlier legal-information infrastructure to current AI capabilities. He offers this as a belief about model training provenance, without identifying models or documenting their training datasets.
qs: we have good reason to believe a lot of the foundation models were able to take all that case law and a lot of their legal knowledge comes from the Case Law Access Project
We couldn't imagine that these large language models would come, consume all that case law and be able to answer a lot of questions about US law

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Reed argues that AI's main professional value is reducing information-finding and organising work so lawyers can concentrate on reasoning and advice, rather than replacing their decision-making role.
pts.d: He revises his earlier idea that a 'third wave' of legal technology would fundamentally change what lawyers do: AI may instead enable lawyers to perform the higher-value work they were always intended to do. He describes digitisation as having burdened lawyers with more information than they could readily process. His preferred model is augmentation, with lawyers remaining responsible for interpretation, decisions and counsel.

pts.k: Reed says Ask Knowable already enables conversational querying of executed contracts and reconstruction of controlling provisions across related documents.
pts.d: He describes natural-language interaction as a transformational change in how lawyers use software. In his account, the system combines curated contract metadata with LLM interpretation of questions, rather than asking an LLM to independently read an entire repository for every answer. He also says it can trace changes through master agreements and amendments and provide a consolidated account of the currently controlling language.

pts.k: Reed claims reliable legal AI depends on substantial software engineering, clean data, human quality control and use-case-specific legal knowledge—not simply placing generative AI over documents.
pts.d: He says a closed, deduplicated document environment, high-quality metadata and collaboration between lawyers and data scientists improve answers. He describes prompt engineering that supplies the operative relationships between legal documents as especially important. He also warns that poor inputs can produce convincing but bad or incomplete answers, making errors harder to recognise.

pts.k: Reed predicts a limited field of credible generalist legal-AI platforms and favours focused products for specific legal tasks.
pts.d: He regards vendors' attempts to do everything as a competitive risk and argues that different contracting and legal activities need different solutions. He identifies LexisNexis and Thomson Reuters as unusually well positioned because of their data, tools and personnel. His account of a viable broad assistant is an interface routing questions to specialised services, not one LLM doing everything. He acknowledges that assembling best-of-breed tools is expensive and difficult. These are claims about software vendors and buyer choices, not about ALSP delivery of legal work.

pts.k: Reed rejects wholesale near-term associate replacement and says building and maintaining AI still requires substantial human staffing.
pts.d: He characterises the idea of replacing all associates with a bot within two years as hype that will not come true. He allows that some tasks may need fewer people, but emphasises continuing development, supervision, monitoring and improvement. His concern extends to law firms and companies attempting to build their own AI applications.

pts.k: Reed envisages agentic AI proactively managing discrete contract tasks, while cautioning against surrendering control over high-stakes legal work.
pts.d: His hypothetical assistant notices upcoming renewals, offers to retrieve contracts for review and asks whether to send a renewal letter or terminate an agreement. He distinguishes acting on tasks from merely retrieving documents or answering questions. He separately contrasts AI autonomy with agency-law concepts and stresses the control being ceded. These examples are prospective possibilities, not reported deployments of autonomous contract action.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is Reed's product-development experience and qualitative accounts of client use; the interview supplies no measured accuracy or productivity results.
pts.d: Reed draws on work at Ravel, LexisNexis and Knowable, describes human-in-the-loop metadata production, and reports live client questioning. He identifies LexisNexis's North American legal team as Ask Knowable's first alpha users and describes a client's 800-document contract family to illustrate complexity. These support his account as practitioner and vendor testimony, not independent performance validation. His staffing, market-structure and agentic predictions are reasoned judgments without quantified supporting studies in the document. His affiliation matters: he is Knowable's CEO and says he remains closely involved with LexisNexis. The host's unverified ChatGPT research anecdote and the separately quoted $10,000-hour forecast are not treated as Reed's own findings or predictions.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Reed distinguishes currently available capabilities from an ongoing transformation, without a firm completion date.
pts.d: At the 2025 interview, Ask Knowable is live and being used by clients; the conversation places its initial generative-AI launch in the preceding November. Reed says the AI-led wave he identified in 2015 is still unfolding and may not yet have crested. His explicit near-term rejection concerns replacing all associates within two years. Broader gains depend on patience, learning, defined use cases, clean data, metadata, legal input and ongoing monitoring as foundation models change. He supplies no date for the prospective agentic contract workflow or eventual broad adoption.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate focus is enterprise contracting teams, with wider implications for lawyers, associates, legal-AI vendors and organisations building their own tools.
pts.d: Large enterprises and their in-house lawyers gain access to organised executed agreements and potentially spend less time locating and reconciling provisions. Lawyers remain interpreters and advisers, while associates are not expected to disappear wholesale in the stated near term. Legal departments and law firms must choose tools matched to their use cases and account for ongoing development and oversight if building internally. Lawyers, data scientists, engineers and product managers remain involved in producing dependable systems. Vendors face competition between specialised tools and resource-rich platforms. The document does not make a concrete claim about unmet civil legal need, consumer access to justice or firm staffing-shape changes.
